explainedBy: The manager hands employees a physical printed card that encourages self-checking.

storyboard.claim: The manager gives out a printed card.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The manager reaches for the single printed sheet and hands it over.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the topic with the physical card.
storyboard.addedInformation: The card is the one-page goal, not a rule.
storyboard.staging: Manager picks up the sheet of paper he always carries.

explainedBy: The card tells each employee to compare their own actions with their goals.

storyboard.claim: The card asks the employee to check goals against actions.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The manager still holds the card, now read as the goal.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same card, now its instruction.
storyboard.addedInformation: Quote on the card, paraphrased as the goal check.
storyboard.staging: Manager keeps holding the sheet while the instruction is spoken.

explainedBy: Employees calibrate their own behavior against the goal shown on one page, with no manager needed.

storyboard.claim: Employees check their own behavior against the goal.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young employee in front of the goal target.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The card now belongs to the employee.
storyboard.staging: Employee faces the goal target alone.

explainedBy: If employees manage themselves, the narrator asks what the manager does with the freed time.

storyboard.claim: A logistical question: what is left for the manager?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The manager, worried, with the question carried in the callout.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shifts from the card to the question.
storyboard.addedInformation: The question is the host's, not a fact.
storyboard.staging: Manager looks concerned at the question.

explainedBy: The three secrets each take one minute, so the manager's time question is about the rest of the day.

storyboard.claim: Each of the three secrets takes one minute.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A clock with the manager beside it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets the timing that raises the question.
storyboard.addedInformation: Timing per intervention, not a deadline.
storyboard.staging: Manager stands with the clock on the wall behind him.

explainedBy: The narrator jokes about what a manager with spare time would do: golf or browse LinkedIn.

storyboard.claim: What does the manager do with free time: golf or LinkedIn?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Manager holding a phone, the LinkedIn joke.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The question becomes concrete.
storyboard.addedInformation: Rhetorical joke, not a claim about this manager.
storyboard.staging: Manager looks at a phone in hand.

explainedBy: Comparison: 20 minutes a day of one-minute interventions against the rest of a 10-person team's workday.

storyboard.claim: Twenty minutes of intervention leaves seven hours forty for other work.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two buckets: the small intervention time and the much larger rest.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the question into a comparison.
storyboard.addedInformation: Numbers from the narration for a team of ten.
storyboard.staging: Sorter with two buckets, no people.

explainedBy: The narrator says this is where the paradigm shift happens: the freed time changes the manager's job.

storyboard.claim: The freed time is a paradigm shift for the manager.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A lightbulb beside the talking manager.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the comparison to its meaning.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shift in thinking, not a literal change.
storyboard.staging: Manager talks with a lightbulb beside him.

explainedBy: A manager who hoards decisions controls every piece of work: the puppeteer is the control.

storyboard.claim: Stop controlling every decision.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The manager as puppeteer, controlling the work.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the habit the manager must drop.
storyboard.addedInformation: The habit is the manager's own control.
storyboard.staging: Manager stands with the puppeteer icon.

explainedBy: Hours spent fixing mistakes that a one-minute redirect would have prevented weeks earlier.

storyboard.claim: Hours go into untangling mistakes a redirect could have prevented.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The manager slumped and worried over the mess.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The cost of not redirecting early.
storyboard.staging: Worried manager slumps.

explainedBy: The highest-leverage use of recovered time is looking ahead to what is coming.

storyboard.claim: Recovered time goes to looking ahead.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A compass held by the manager, direction forward.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Where the recovered time goes.
storyboard.staging: Manager stands with the compass.

explainedBy: The manager lifts his head to look six months and two years ahead.

storyboard.claim: Look six months and two years ahead.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same compass, manager points forward.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same compass, now looking forward.
storyboard.staging: Manager points ahead with the compass kept.

explainedBy: The time is spent developing more people who will become winners.

storyboard.claim: Recovered time develops potential winners.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A trophy beside the manager.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From looking ahead to developing people.
storyboard.addedInformation: Winners are people, not a prize.
storyboard.staging: Manager with the trophy icon.

explainedBy: The manager actively mentors an inexperienced person beside him.

storyboard.claim: A manager mentors an inexperienced employee.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Manager talks to the young employee.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The freed time becomes mentoring.
storyboard.staging: Manager talks warmly to the young employee.

explainedBy: The manager praises the employee for doing something approximately right.

storyboard.claim: Catch the employee doing something right.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same pair; the manager celebrates the employee's small win.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same pair, now the praise.
storyboard.staging: Manager celebrates beside the young employee.

explainedBy: Cause and effect: the upfront investment in short honest moments fuels the self-management engine.

storyboard.claim: Upfront investment fuels self-management.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow from investment to self-management.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the praise pair matters.
storyboard.addedInformation: Cause and effect from the narration.
storyboard.staging: Flow diagram, no people.

explainedBy: The sequence of being nice versus tough is a failure state that needs a fixed order.

storyboard.claim: The order of nice and tough matters.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A balance weighing nice against tough.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns to the second failure state.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sequence, not a balance of equal weights.
storyboard.staging: Balance icon, no people.

explainedBy: The narrator introduces a parable about getting the nice-tough sequence wrong.
noVisual: No emperor cast key; the parable stays as text over the same balance.

storyboard.claim: A parable shows the fatal flaw.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same balance, parable named.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same balance, now the parable.
storyboard.staging: Balance kept while the parable is introduced.

explainedBy: An emperor wants to be the benevolent nice guy who gives rewards.
noVisual: No emperor cast key; gift icon carries the niceness.

storyboard.claim: The emperor wants to be the nice guy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A gift, the rewards the emperor gives.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The parable begins with the emperor.
storyboard.staging: Gift icon, no people.

explainedBy: The emperor splits the roles: he rewards and praises, the prime minister taxes and punishes.

storyboard.claim: Rewards go to the emperor, punishments to the minister.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two buckets: rewarding versus punishing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the nice guy into a split.
storyboard.addedInformation: Split of roles from the narration.
storyboard.staging: Sorter with two buckets, no people.

explainedBy: The emperor hands the bad-guy role to the prime minister, a good cop, bad cop split.

storyboard.claim: The emperor assigns the bad-guy role.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same sorter; the callout names the role.
storyboard.onScreenText: The bad-guy role is handed over
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same split, now named.
storyboard.staging: Sorter kept, callout names the role.

explainedBy: When the emperor asks for something, people smile at him but ignore him.
noVisual: No emperor cast key; the ignoring has no vocabulary icon, so text carries it.

storyboard.claim: People smile but do not act on his requests.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Empty stage with the callout.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The split fails when asked to act.
storyboard.staging: No people; the callout carries the contrast.

explainedBy: People ignore the emperor because they do not fear him.
noVisual: No emperor cast key; text-led contrast kept from the beat before.

storyboard.claim: They do not fear the emperor.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same empty stage, callout names the missing fear.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why they ignore him.
storyboard.staging: No people; the callout carries the missing fear.

explainedBy: When the terrifying prime minister speaks, people obey: he controls them.

storyboard.claim: The prime minister holds the real power.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Puppeteer icon: one person controlling others.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrast with the ignored emperor.
storyboard.staging: Puppeteer icon, no people.

explainedBy: In a panic the emperor tries to switch roles with the prime minister.
noVisual: Switching roles between two people has no vocabulary icon; the callout names it.

storyboard.claim: The emperor switches roles.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Empty stage with the callout.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reaction to losing power.
storyboard.staging: No people; callout carries the switch.

explainedBy: The emperor asks the minister to take the rewards so he can get his power back.
noVisual: No emperor cast key; the speech is carried by the callout.

storyboard.claim: The emperor wants his power back.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Empty stage with the callout.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the reason for the switch.
storyboard.staging: No people; callout carries the motive.

explainedBy: Within a month the people revolt violently against the switched emperor.
noVisual: A crowd revolt cannot be drawn: the crowd shot repeats one person; text carries it.

storyboard.claim: The switch causes a violent revolt.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Empty stage with the callout.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Consequence of the switch.
storyboard.staging: No people; the callout carries the revolt.

explainedBy: Cause and effect: the nice emperor who gave up his tough role is overthrown.

storyboard.claim: The nice emperor is overthrown.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow from nice emperor to overthrown.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The consequence of the revolt.
storyboard.addedInformation: The prime minister becomes emperor, stated in narration.
storyboard.staging: Flow diagram, no people.

explainedBy: The narrator states the lesson for leadership: the order is exact.

storyboard.claim: The leadership lesson is exact.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Lightbulb beside the talking manager.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the parable to the lesson.
storyboard.staging: Manager talks beside the lightbulb.

explainedBy: Being a buddy first, soft and accommodating, sets a baseline that makes later toughness feel wrong.

storyboard.claim: A buddy-first baseline sets up later problems.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Manager and young employee in a warm talk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Back to office; buddy-first setup.
storyboard.addedInformation: Warmth is genuine here; the problem is the order.
storyboard.staging: Warm talk between manager and employee.

explainedBy: The buddy-first setup becomes a baseline, so enforcing accountability later does not feel like management.

storyboard.claim: Buddy-first becomes the baseline.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same pair; the manager slumps, worried.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same pair, now the baseline problem.
storyboard.staging: Manager slumps, worried, beside the young employee.

explainedBy: The employee feels betrayed when accountability arrives after a buddy-first baseline.

storyboard.claim: The employee feels betrayed by the new accountability.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Young employee, sad, slumped.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The baseline turns into betrayal.
storyboard.addedInformation: Feeling is the employee's, quoted from the narration.
storyboard.staging: Young employee slumps, sad.
